subject: English
passage: Roman sculptors in the first and second centuries often depicted elaborate banquet scenes featuring expensive delicacies like peacock and imported spices. Some historians, noting that bread and porridge were staple foods for most Romans, interpret these sculptural depictions as reflections of typical Roman dining practices. However, a team of researchers recently analyzed hundreds of food-related sculptures and discovered that saffron—which could only be obtained in Rome at enormous expense, since it had to be imported from distant provinces—appears in Roman sculptures of the period more than four times as frequently as bread does, thereby casting doubt on the idea that ______
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: depictions of food in Roman sculptures of the period should be taken as realistic representations of Roman dining practices.
choices.B: bread was a more significant component of the Roman diet of the period than saffron was.
choices.C: food was a more popular subject among Roman sculptors than it was among artists from other civilizations at the time.
choices.D: Roman sculptors of the period may have depicted foods for symbolic reasons rather than to show what Romans typically ate.

explanation:
Choice A is the best answer because it identifies what the research findings call into question. The text explains that some historians interpret food depictions in Roman sculptures as reflections of typical dining practices. The text goes on to present contradictory evidence: saffron, an expensive imported product, appears more frequently in sculptures than bread, a staple food. Because it's unlikely that expensive saffron was consumed more often than basic bread, this frequency mismatch casts doubt on the theory that sculptures realistically depicted Roman dining habits.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect because the text suggests the opposite: it states that bread was a staple food for most Romans, while saffron was an expensive import, so bread was clearly more significant in the actual Roman diet.
